newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Peace talks after bloody Sierra Leone clashes.
newsitem.headline: Peace talks after bloody Sierra Leone clashes.

text.p: Commanders of West African soldiers in Sierra Leone held talks with military ruler Major Johnny Paul Koroma on Monday after over a day of bloody clashes between his forces and Nigerian troops south of the capital.

Military officials in Freetown said that Nigerian, Ghanaian and Guinean commanders were taking part in the talks, which included other members of the junta installed after a May 25 coup toppled President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

Nigerian troops and soldiers loyal to Sierra Leone's military rulers fought with heavy weapons around Jui south of Freetown late on Saturday and on Sunday, sending several thousand civilians fleeing from their homes, witnesses said.

Residents of Jui, Benguema and Hastings, towns in the thick of fighting, talk of bodies of soldiers and civilians lying in the streets. Witnesses and military sources say the clashes killed more than 20 soldiers or civilians caught in crossfire.

The fighting pitting Nigerians in Jui against the newly constituted People's Army -- soldiers supporting the coup plus rebel who rallied to their cause -- eased late on Sunday. There was no immediate word on the results of the talks.
State radio accused a Nigerian plane of bombing a residential area on Sunday killing four people and wounding 50.
The cause of the clashes some 15 miles (24 km) southeast of Freetown near Hastings airport was not immediately clear.

The Nigerian commander of West African soldiers in Sierra Leone and Liberia, General Victor Malu, rejected suggestions that Nigerian troops started the fighting. "We had no reason to attack them," he told BBC radio.

The two sides also clashed on Wednesday and Thursday at Lungi international airport, across an estuary from the capital as members of the People's Army hunted for a clandestine radio station that has broadcast messages from Kabbah.
Nigeria, which had troops in the country under a defence pact before the coup, has sent reinforcements as part of efforts to persuade the military junta to restore Kabbah to power.

Lungi residents said that Nigerians troops with tanks took control of the whole town over the weekend, driving back Sierra Leonian soldiers and rebel fighters. Residents say 200 people, mostly rebels, were killed in the midweek Lungi clashes.
Impoverished Sierra Leone's West African neighbours have agreed to try dialogue and economic sanctions as methods of persuasion, but have retained the military option.
Military sources say there are 10,000 mostly Nigerian West African troops now in Sierra Leone.
Kabbah came to power in 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of military rule. Rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup -- the third in five years.
